exercise.name: Band Decline Sit-up

reference.title: Band Decline Sit-up
reference.listing: Video (title and number from the catalog listing; the page could not be read from this environment, so the movement follows the exercise name and standard coaching)

equipment: Decline bench (slant board with ankle roller)

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl and sit up, inhale as you lower under control.
breathing.cadence: About 1.6 s up, a short pause, about 2 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1.5 s up, brief pause, 2 s down
prescription.progression: Steeper board, slower lowering, then a light load

cues.text: Lie on the decline board head-down, feet hooked under the roller; hands behind the head holding the ends of two bands anchored low at the head end of the bench, elbows wide.
Breathe out, tuck the chin a little and curl the head and shoulder blades off the board.
Keep curling and sit up toward the knees against the bands; hands stay behind the head.
Pause with the chest close to the thighs, bands taut.
Breathe in and roll back down slowly: low back first, then the shoulder blades, head last.
Rest the shoulders on the board for a moment; repeat.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling the head forward with the hands
mistakes.fix: Hands stay lightly behind the head, elbows wide; the trunk does the work.

mistakes.mistake: Sitting up with a flat back from the hips
mistakes.fix: Curl the head and shoulders first.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the bands yank you back down
Feet slipping out from under the roller

kinematics.measure: Trunk (pelvis to C7) from the board
kinematics.norm: From lying on the board to sitting up close to the thighs (J Strength Cond Res 2015)
Low back curls early and stays rounded at the top (clinical opinion)
Most of the second half of a sit-up is hip flexion (Andersson 1997)
The bands add load that grows as the trunk rises (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #008997, Band Decline Sit-up, video (movement reference)
Escamilla et al. 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379)
Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
Andersson, Nilsson, Ma and Thorstensson 1997, abdominal and hip flexor muscle activation during various training exercises (Eur J Appl Physiol 75:115-123; PMID 9118976)
Effect of traditional vs modified bent-knee sit-up on abdominal and hip flexor muscle EMG activity (J Strength Cond Res 29(12):3472-3479, 2015; PMID 25970493)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.

Lying head-down raises pressure in the head; skip the decline with uncontrolled high blood pressure, glaucoma or a recent eye or head problem (clinical opinion), and sit up slowly at the end of the set.
Check that the roller is locked and the feet are hooked before lying back.
Full sit-ups load the low back more than curl-ups (McGill 1998; Axler and McGill 1997).
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion and twisting.
Check the bands and anchors before each set; a snapped band can hit the head.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Neck pain: cross the arms on the chest.
Low-back discomfort: stop at a crunch.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the trunk off the board: about 40% (upper) and 35% (lower) MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up (Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris pull the trunk up once the shoulder blades are off the board; anchored feet raise hip-flexor activity (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.obliques: External obliques steady the trunk on the way up and down (Escamilla 2016; Konrad 2001).
